items.explain: The person picks up the appointment card, keeps a shelter bed, and finally attends a clinic chest X-ray.
The person learns the long cough is probably tuberculosis and starts months of treatment from the local pharmacy.
Using the shelter as a mailing address, they get benefits restored, likely with job-search rules eased for health reasons.
The person loses the shelter bed, sleeps rough under an underpass again, and often misses picking up medicine.
The person stops taking medicine, the illness worsens, and they end up in emergency hospital care.
They try for warehouse or agency jobs, but without a home and with poor health get only occasional cash work.
The person is expected to die in 2058, aged 52, from tuberculosis and living outdoors.
The person sleeps outside in the cold and their health declines, though a shelter place may now reduce this.
The person refuses a sibling's offer of money or a home elsewhere, wanting to stay near familiar places and memories.
The person catches a lung infection from someone coughing badly in the shelter or library.
The person may finally be offered social housing after years of waiting, but only if a hold is lifted.
The person dies of a stroke from high blood pressure around age 75, still in a shelter or temporary housing.
The person is expected to die in 2060, aged 75, from a stroke caused by high blood pressure.
Social workers assess the family and find the damp home and child's wheezing, not neglect, are the real problem.
The person pushes a housing complaint in person and gets drawn into a tenants' protest group.
The family must meet conditions on home and school attendance, and the threat of losing the child remains.
Debt collectors pursue an old loan, and repayments squeeze money already reduced by rent deductions.
After long pushing, they get moved out of the damp flat because of the child's breathing problems.
The person leaves an insecure care job after depression and unpaid travel strain, still taking antidepressants.
They return to care work with guaranteed hours, benefit rules loosen, and household life becomes more stable.
The person is diagnosed with a lasting lung disease, caused by years of damp housing and smoke.
The person dies at 66 after a sudden lung flare-up, worsened by heart problems.
The person is expected to die in 2088, aged 66, from a flare-up of chronic lung disease.
The person attends a permitted protest outside the council building, but fewer people turn up than hoped.
They try to officially register a tenants' group, but it likely stalls for lack of members.
With no income since losing driving work, unpaid tax and fines are passed to bailiffs.
The person refuses to pay a disputed monthly charge, and the council starts eviction proceedings.
They avoid eviction by agreeing to repay arrears, and their activism shrinks to writing letters.
At 59, with no car and poor transport, they stay jobless and live on benefits until pension age.
They refuse a steady-hours yard job and stay in agency warehouse work, earning partly on the books.
The person loses agency warehouse work as the company automates, just like a previous layoff.
They go back to undeclared cash work, old contacts and nights under the bridge, partly checked by a mentor.
The person is arrested and convicted again for theft or drugs, which will show up on job checks.
The person moves to another town for warehouse work and drops out of the city's records.
They live on low income with unstable housing for years, getting only short-term delivery jobs.
The person dies of heart disease linked to years of poverty and night shifts.
Reducing methadone could lead to a relapse and overdose, so the dose is held and overdose antidote provided.
The person stays on a stable methadone dose with supervised doses and keeps testing drug-free.
The person is turned down as a children's reading volunteer because of past convictions, losing a positive routine.
They complete their suspended sentence without trouble, but police still stop and search them locally.
The person sees their child and grandchild again at Christmas, as long as they stay drug-free.
The person loses informal scrapyard work, lives only on benefits, and is tempted by metal theft again.
After losing income, the person is arrested again for theft or handling stolen goods; outcome unclear.
The person relapses on opioids and dies alone at home from an overdose.
The person is expected to die in 2059, aged 65, from an opioid overdose.
Their child moves away to university, leaving two adults who already rarely connect.
The person takes a sideways role with a small raise, still under a workplace rival.
A blood pressure crisis sends the person to a clinic and reveals a drinking problem, though work health support may prevent it.
The person's supervisor job is automated away, just as they once did to others.
The person is diagnosed with long-term heart disease after years of high blood pressure, little sleep and drinking.
Home delivery stops, so the person must collect antidepressants at the clinic, sometimes with a neighbour's help.
The person rewrites their will alone, likely leaving everything to a child abroad or a hospice.
A young neighbour who collected prescriptions moves away, leaving the person with less help.
The person stops eating and collecting medicine, then falls or becomes malnourished and is taken to hospital.
The neighbour's help fades, doctor visits become irregular, and the person stops collecting medicine.
The person is expected to die in 2055, aged 86, from a heart problem and frailty.
The person takes a refused information request about computer-run housing decisions to an outside appeal.
The person shares handwritten notes showing suspicious city patterns, likely with a young friend or journalist.
The relationship ends formally because the partner's job secrecy rules make living together impossible.
The person leaves the city, probably for another town, and becomes much harder to track.
The person quits the head librarian job, leaving regular library users with less support.
They keep quietly campaigning for public access to records and openness about computer decisions.
The person retires from library work around age 65.
